explanations.answer: The word of the LORD is rare
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The text says "the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce." In plain words, hearing from God was not an everyday thing in those days. It was quieter than my bakery when the oven timer finally stops.

explanations.answer: No rain has fallen in years
explanations.explanation: The writer never mentions rain here, friend. What the text says is that the word of the LORD was rare and visions were scarce. Nobody in this scene is checking a weather app. The drought is in the hearing, not the sky.

explanations.answer: The lamp of God stays dark
explanations.explanation: Close, because the lamp does show up in the next verse. But the text says this happens "Before the lamp of God had gone out," so it was still burning. The thing that was scarce was the word of the LORD, along with visions. That's the difference in those days.

Yes, the temple of the LORD. The text puts Samuel lying down there, right where the ark of God was located. That's a pretty special place to be tucked in for the night. I've slept in a junk drawer, so I'm in no position to judge anyone's bedroom.

No mountain in this scene. The text says Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located. Climbing to bed every night would be a lot of work for a boy. Good news, he didn't have to.

Not a garden. The text says Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located. Sleeping out in a garden would have been a whole other night of noises. This boy was indoors.

Right. He runs to Eli and says, "Here I am, for you have called me." He's sure it's Eli's voice. The text says later that Samuel "did not yet know the LORD" (1 Samuel 3:7), so he had no way to guess who else it could be.

It's actually true. Samuel ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you have called me." He wouldn't say that if he thought someone else was calling. The text says Samuel "did not yet know the LORD" (1 Samuel 3:7), so Eli was the only voice he figured it could be.
That's it. Eli says, "I did not call… Go back and lie down." Short, simple and sleepy. I think Eli just wants the boy to get some rest.
Eli doesn't hand out a night shift here. He tells Samuel to go back and lie down. Samuel obeys and goes right back to bed.

Eli doesn't say anything about praying at this point. His words are, "Go back and lie down." The praying comes up later, when Eli tells Samuel what to say if the voice calls again. For now, it's just bedtime.
Not quite. The text says Samuel "got up, went to Eli," and said again, "Here I am, for you have called me." He didn't lie there waiting to hear it a second time. That boy was up and moving.
Right, he doesn't stay put. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you have called me." Eli answered, "My son, I did not call." This kid was running laps in the dark.

explanations.answer: The word of the LORD hasn't been revealed to him
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The text says Samuel "did not yet know the LORD, because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him." That's why he keeps running to Eli. He just hadn't been through this before.

explanations.answer: He hasn't been brought into the temple of the LORD
explanations.explanation: He's already there. The text says Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located. What hasn't happened yet is that the word of the LORD hasn't been revealed to him. That's the reason for the running.

explanations.answer: He hasn't started serving the LORD before Eli
explanations.explanation: He's already serving. The very first verse says the boy Samuel "ministered to the LORD before Eli." What hasn't happened is the word of the LORD being revealed to him (1 Samuel 3:7). Different thing entirely.
Yes, on the third call. The text says, "Then Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy." It took three rounds, but Eli put it together. Eli, the priest, finally connected the dots.
It's true, friend. The text says, "Then Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy." It took a few trips down that hallway. But he got there.

explanations.answer: Ask the LORD to speak because he's listening
explanations.explanation: That's it. Eli says to tell Him, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." Short and simple. Samuel doesn't need a speech, just open ears.

explanations.answer: Ask the LORD to tell him who He is
explanations.explanation: Eli doesn't give Samuel that line. The words he gives are, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." Samuel is meant to listen, not quiz the voice. Eli keeps it plain.

explanations.answer: Ask the LORD to come back in the morning
explanations.explanation: Nothing about putting it off. Eli says to answer, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." The plan is to listen right then. No rescheduling in these words.

explanations.answer: The LORD comes and stands there
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says, "Then the LORD came and stood there, calling as before, 'Samuel! Samuel!'" This time He doesn't just call from a distance. He's right there with the boy.
Not through Eli. Eli is back in his room and the text says the LORD Himself "came and stood there." Eli told Samuel what to say, but the calling came from the LORD.
No angel in this verse. The text says, "the LORD came and stood there, calling as before." He comes Himself. That's what makes this fourth call different.
Yes, Eli, the priest. The LORD says, "On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end." This is a heavy word. It's about Eli's house.
Not Samuel. He's the one hearing the message, not the one it's about. The LORD says He will carry out His word "against Eli… about his house." Samuel is just holding hard news.

Elkanah was Samuel's father (1 Samuel 1:19-20), but he doesn't come up in this passage. The LORD names Eli: "I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house." That's the name on this message.

explanations.answer: His sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them
explanations.explanation: That's what the LORD says. "His sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them." It's the iniquity "of which he knows." This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: He stopped offering the yearly sacrifices at the temple
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that. He says Eli's sons blasphemed God and Eli did not restrain them. Nothing here mentions yearly sacrifices stopping. It's a different charge.

explanations.answer: He let the lamp of God go out in the temple
explanations.explanation: The lamp doesn't come up as the charge. Earlier the text only says the lamp of God had not gone out yet (1 Samuel 3:3). The LORD names this instead: his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them.
It's the other way around, and it's a hard line. The LORD says, "The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering." No amount is named. I think this one hurts.

Right, and this one is heavy. The LORD says, "The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering." Sacrifice and offering are both named, and neither covers it. It's a sober verse.
Yes. The text says Samuel "was afraid to tell Eli the vision." I think anyone would feel that with a message like this. It's a hard thing to carry to someone you know.
No, it's the opposite. The text says Samuel "was afraid to tell Eli the vision." I think that makes sense with such a hard message. Nobody is rushing to deliver that.
The text doesn't say anyone forbade him. It says Samuel "was afraid to tell Eli the vision." The feeling is fear. Nobody gave him an order to keep quiet.
Yes. Eli says, "Do not hide it from me." He also asks for "anything He said to you." He wants all of it.

explanations.answer: Only the parts about his sons
explanations.explanation: Eli asks for much more than that. He says, "May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you." The word is anything. He's not picking out parts.

explanations.answer: A short summary for later on
explanations.explanation: Eli isn't asking for a summary. He says, "Do not hide it from me," and warns about hiding "anything He said to you." He wants the whole message right then.
It's the other way around. The text says, "Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him." He was afraid, but he said all of it. That's a lot of courage for a boy.
Right. The text says, "Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him." Nothing softened and nothing left out. Even afraid, he told it all.

explanations.answer: He says let the LORD do what He sees as good
explanations.explanation: That's Eli's answer. He says, "He is the LORD… Let Him do what is good in His eyes." It's a calm reply after hard news. I think that took something.

explanations.answer: He argues that the message is not fair to him
explanations.explanation: Eli doesn't argue. After hearing everything, he says, "He is the LORD… Let Him do what is good in His eyes." No fight in those words.

explanations.answer: He tells Samuel to keep the whole thing quiet
explanations.explanation: Eli doesn't say that. He had asked to hear it all, and then he replied, "He is the LORD… Let Him do what is good in His eyes." No hush order in the text.

explanations.answer: The LORD lets none of them fall to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's how it reads. The text says the LORD "let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground." Every word counted. It's a good sign for the boy who kept running to the wrong room.

explanations.answer: The LORD makes all of them echo through the land
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say echo. It says the LORD "let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground." His words didn't drop. Nobody's yelling in a canyon here.

explanations.answer: The LORD lets each of them shine like a lamp
explanations.explanation: The lamp is back in 1 Samuel 3:3, and it isn't about Samuel's words. What the text says is that the LORD "let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground." That's the picture.
Yes, prophet. The text says all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel "was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD." The whole land knew. News traveled that way back then too.
Not king. Samuel is "confirmed as a prophet of the LORD." This passage never calls him a king. All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew him as a prophet.
No desk job on this one. The text says all Israel knew Samuel "was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD." Scribe isn't the word. The word is prophet.
Yes. The text says, "the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word." Back in verse 1, the word was rare. Now it keeps showing up.

It's true, friend. The text says, "the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word." Early on, the word of the LORD was rare (1 Samuel 3:1). Now it keeps coming to Samuel.
